title: Data Distribution
summary: Spreading one dataset across many machines. 5 building blocks drilled by recall: the signal that says reach for one, what it costs, how it breaks, which sibling rules it out, and what it is doing across the canonical problems.
keyTakeaways: Sharding — Splitting one logical dataset across many machines by a partition key, so capacity and throughput scale horizontally.
Replication — Keeping copies of the same data on multiple nodes, for read capacity, fault tolerance, or geographic proximity.
Consistent Hashing — Placing keys and nodes on a ring so adding or removing a node moves only ~1/N of keys instead of remapping everything.
Quorum (N/W/R) — Requiring W acknowledgements to write and R responses to read out of N replicas, tuning consistency against availability.
Distributed ID Generation — Producing unique identifiers across many machines without a central allocator — Snowflake-style, UUID, or ranged counters.

questions.prompt: Sharding vs Consistent Hashing vs Replication — what decides between them?
points: Consistent Hashing — The placement scheme that makes adding and removing shards cheap; sharding is the what, this is the how.
Replication — If reads are the bottleneck and the data fits, replicas scale reads without splitting anything.
Sharding — Splitting one logical dataset across many machines by a partition key, so capacity and throughput scale horizontally.
questions.answer: Consistent Hashing: The placement scheme that makes adding and removing shards cheap; sharding is the what, this is the how. Replication: If reads are the bottleneck and the data fits, replicas scale reads without splitting anything.

questions.prompt: Sharding appears in 7 of the canonical design problems. Name as many as you can, and say what it is doing in each.
points: Design a URL Shortener — Splits the mapping table by short-code hash once one primary cannot hold the row count. Access is pure key lookup, which shards about as cleanly as anything does.
Design a Leaderboard — Partitions scores by leaderboard and time window; one global sorted set would concentrate every write in the system on a single node.
Design a Typeahead / Autocomplete Service — The trie is partitioned by prefix — the textbook uneven partition, since 'a' and 'th' carry orders of magnitude more traffic than 'zq'.
Design a Distributed Key-Value Store — The core mechanic. The keyspace is divided across nodes by ring position, and every other feature in the design is built on top of that division.
Design a Proximity Service — Geo cells are the partition key, so nearby entities land on the same node. Locality is the point; population skew is the price you agree to pay.
Design a Search Engine — The index is split document-wise so each shard holds a slice of the corpus; a query scatters to every shard and gathers the top-K.
Design an Observability Platform — Telemetry is partitioned by series or tenant, because ingest volume is the defining constraint and no single node absorbs a firehose.

questions.prompt: Replication vs Quorum (N/W/R) vs Sharding — what decides between them?
points: Quorum (N/W/R) — Quorum reads/writes let you tune the consistency-availability point instead of accepting the default.
Sharding — Replication scales reads; sharding scales writes and capacity. Most real systems need both.
Replication — Keeping copies of the same data on multiple nodes, for read capacity, fault tolerance, or geographic proximity.
questions.answer: Quorum (N/W/R): Quorum reads/writes let you tune the consistency-availability point instead of accepting the default. Sharding: Replication scales reads; sharding scales writes and capacity. Most real systems need both.

questions.prompt: Replication appears in 6 of the canonical design problems. Name as many as you can, and say what it is doing in each.
points: Design a Distributed Cache — Each entry is held on N successive ring nodes, so losing one node degrades the hit rate instead of losing a whole slice of the keyspace.
Design a Payment System (Wallet / Ledger) — Synchronous replication of the ledger, because losing an acknowledged financial write is not a degraded mode — it is an unrecoverable defect.
Design a Distributed Message Queue — Each partition has a leader and followers; the in-sync replica set is what lets an acknowledged publish survive a broker dying.
Design a Distributed Key-Value Store — N replicas per key range with tunable W and R — where this problem's entire consistency-versus-availability conversation actually lives.
Design a Search Engine — Index shards are replicated for read throughput and node loss. Query volume, not durability, is what drives the replica count here.
Design an Authentication & Session Service — Session state is replicated across regions, so a login in one region is honoured in another without a cross-region read on every request.

Query volume, not durability, is what drives the replica count here. in Design an Authentication & Session Service, session state is replicated across regions, so a login in one region is honoured in another without a cross-region read on every request.

Clients disagreeing about ring membership and writing the same key to different nodes

questions.prompt: Consistent Hashing vs Sharding vs Hot-Key Mitigation — what decides between them?
points: Sharding — Range-based sharding when you need ordered scans and can accept manual rebalancing.
Hot-Key Mitigation — The ring balances key COUNT, never key DEMAND — pair it with hot-key handling.
Consistent Hashing — Placing keys and nodes on a ring so adding or removing a node moves only ~1/N of keys instead of remapping everything.
questions.answer: Sharding: Range-based sharding when you need ordered scans and can accept manual rebalancing. Hot-Key Mitigation: The ring balances key COUNT, never key DEMAND — pair it with hot-key handling.

questions.prompt: Consistent Hashing appears in 3 of the canonical design problems. Name as many as you can, and say what it is doing in each.
points: Design a Distributed Rate Limiter — Routes each client key to the node holding its counter, so limiter state is not remapped every time a gateway is added or removed.
Design a Distributed Cache — Places keys on the ring so adding a node moves ~1/N of them, instead of invalidating the whole cache and stampeding the origin.
Design a Distributed Key-Value Store — Assigns key ranges to nodes and defines the replica set as the next N nodes clockwise from the key's ring position.

questions.prompt: Quorum (N/W/R) vs Replication vs Conflict Resolution — what decides between them?
points: Replication — Plain leader-follower replication when you do not need per-request tuning.
Conflict Resolution — Quorums make concurrent writes possible; something still has to decide who wins.
Quorum (N/W/R) — Requiring W acknowledgements to write and R responses to read out of N replicas, tuning consistency against availability.

questions.prompt: Quorum (N/W/R) appears in 3 of the canonical design problems. Name as many as you can, and say what it is doing in each.
points: Design a Distributed Cache — Read and write acknowledgement counts decide whether a cached value may be stale — the tunable this design exposes to its callers.
Design a Payment System (Wallet / Ledger) — W and R are set so an acknowledged ledger write survives losing a replica; latency is spent deliberately to buy that guarantee.
Design a Distributed Key-Value Store — Tunable N/W/R is the interface through which this design exposes the consistency-availability tradeoff to its callers.

questions.prompt: Distributed ID Generation vs Relational Database vs Consistent Hashing — what decides between them?
points: Relational Database — A single auto-increment column is correct and boring until you actually outgrow one primary.
Consistent Hashing — If the id only needs to route, hashing an existing natural key may remove the problem.
Distributed ID Generation — Producing unique identifiers across many machines without a central allocator — Snowflake-style, UUID, or ranged counters.
